title: The Trough
scene: He comes back without a solution.

paragraphs: The kitchen light was brighter than he wanted.
Mukund stood with both hands on the counter. There was nothing left to wash.
On his phone, the venue had replied. A room might be available the following weekend. They wanted dates, numbers and a deposit.
He opened the message. Behind him, a cupboard hinge gave a small click as the door settled.
He left the reply box empty.
When he returned, Aarna was holding the sheet of paper with the cross on it.
"I was going to photograph it," she said.
"The one by the window?"
She nodded.
"You can still..."
He stopped. She looked at him.
"Sorry."
She folded the paper once and opened it again.
"That thing I said," he began.
"I heard it."
"I wasn't going anywhere."
She smoothed the crease with her thumb.
"It sounded like you wanted me to tell you to."
"I don't."
He stood there until she looked up.
"Can I sit?"
She moved the masking tape.
He sat beside her. His knee clicked again.
"You should get that looked at," she said.
"I thought we weren't fixing things."
She laughed before she could stop herself. It came out thin and surprised.
"I'm sorry about the cloth."
"It's a cloth."
"I know."
For a while they said nothing. She could hear a neighbour moving a chair upstairs.
"Have you really not eaten?" he asked.
"Some toast."
He held up his phone, waiting.
"Food is fine," she said.
While they waited for it, he asked about the opening.
"What about it?"
"You said you'd decided where to stand."
She told him about the bag, then about the shoes she had bought and not worn enough. Her father would have asked what the frames cost. He would have tried to do it quietly.
"My mother would have stopped him."
"Would that have worked?"
"For about four minutes."
She turned Room Enough towards them.
"Do you remember that first place?"
"The one with the heater that sounded like a shopping cart?"
"That's the one."
He leaned closer.
"I thought this was a window."
Her fingers tightened against the frame. Then she pointed.
"That's the hinge."
"Oh."
His sleeve brushed her wrist as he followed the line.
"The door wasn't that wide," he said.
"No."
She showed him the marks where the coat hook had been. She had meant to cover them with a calendar. For the whole year she lived there, she never did.
"I used to hide everything before you came over. The paint, the brushes. You probably thought I was tidy."
"I remember the suitcase."
She looked at him.
"The wheels stuck out."
She laughed again, and then it went wrong. She covered her face.
He touched her elbow.
"Can I?"
She leaned towards him.
He put an arm around her.
The work was good. There would be another exhibition. He could hear the beginnings of both sentences and kept his mouth shut.
Her shoulders moved against him. He had not realised how much effort she had been making to stay quiet.
At one point she apologised for his shirt.
"It's already painted."
She made a sound that might have been a laugh.
His leg went numb. He shifted his weight and moved the phone from his pocket to the floor.
When she sat up, he reached for a tissue and handed her the box instead. She took three.
"I'm still upset," she said.
"I know."
He started to touch her hair, then stopped when she reached for another tissue.
"I didn't mean you hadn't helped."
He nodded. They stayed where they were until the doorbell rang.
